--- title: "Shiny app-packages without a server" subtitle: "New `webR` and `shinyelectron` chapters in Shiny App-Packages" author: "Martin Frigaard" date: "2026-10-15" categories: [Shiny, webR, Deployment] draft: true toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-title: 'Contents' toc-location: right --- I've added two chapters to [Shiny App-Packages](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/) that cover deployments without a server running R. The [webR chapter](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/webr.html) runs the app in the user's browser, and the [shinyelectron chapter](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/shinyelectron.html) packages it as a desktop installer. In this post I'll cover what each chapter does with `sap` (the book's app-package), and the problems I ran into along the way. ## Three places to run an app Every deployment in the earlier chapters (Connect Cloud, Docker, GitHub Actions) needs a server. The new chapters move R onto the user's computer. The diagram below shows where R runs in each case: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 6 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false}}}%% flowchart TD Pkg(["sap
app-package"]) subgraph Srv["Server"] RS("R process on a host
(Connect Cloud, Docker)") end subgraph Web["Browser"] Live[["shinylive::export()"]] WR("webR session
in the browser tab") end subgraph Desk["Desktop"] SE[["shinyelectron::export()"]] EL("Electron window with
portable R or webR") end Pkg -->|"i. deploy"| RS Pkg -->|"ii. export"| Live Live --> WR Pkg -->|"iii. export"| SE SE --> EL style Srv fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style Web fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style Desk fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style Pkg fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style RS fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Live fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style WR fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style SE fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style EL fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 ``` The two chapters build on each other. The desktop chapter reuses the launcher from the browser chapter, and its Linux build depends on the `WebAssembly` binary we set up for the browser. ## webR: the app in a browser tab [`webR`](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) is R compiled to [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/), a binary format that modern browsers run at near native speed. [`shinylive`](https://posit-dev.github.io/r-shinylive/) bundles a Shiny app, `webR`, and the app's packages into a folder of static files. A static file host is just a web server that hands out files without running any code. GitHub Pages or Netlify can serve the app. After the first download, every click stays in the browser. ### What the browser can't do The browser takes on the server's job, and it can't do all of it. I've found these trade-offs matter most: * First load: the browser downloads `webR` and every package before the app appears. * Visible code: all the code and data go to the browser, so never include credentials. * No system tools or downloads: `system()` calls fail, and `sass::font_google()` needs `local = FALSE`. * Temporary files: logs disappear when the tab closes. ### Every package needs a binary `webR` can't install packages from source, so each package in `Imports` needs a `WebAssembly` binary. The chapter checks `DESCRIPTION` against the [`webR` repository](https://repo.r-wasm.org): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} wasm_pkgs <- available.packages( contriburl = "https://repo.r-wasm.org/bin/emscripten/contrib/4.6" ) base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = "base")) imports <- read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = "Imports") imports <- trimws(strsplit(imports, ",")[[1]]) imports <- imports[imports != ""] setdiff(imports, c(rownames(wasm_pkgs), base_pkgs)) ``` ::: An empty result (`character(0)`) means every dependency has a binary. `sap` itself isn't on CRAN, so it has no binary. [R-universe](https://r-universe.dev/) builds one on each push. Setting it up takes a `.r-universe.dev` repository, a `packages.json` file, and the R-universe GitHub app. :::: {.callout-important collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [Install the GitHub app first]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} Nothing builds until the R-universe GitHub app is installed. Use the installation link, not the repository settings. ::: :::: We then install `sap` from the universe, because `shinylive` uses each installed package's source to find its binary. ### A launcher, not `launch_app()` `shinylive` exports a folder with an `app.R` file, not a package. The chapter adds a small launcher in `inst/webr/app.R`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} library(shiny) library(sap) shinyApp( ui = movies_ui(bslib = TRUE), server = movies_server ) ``` ::: The launcher returns a Shiny app object instead of calling `launch_app()`. `launch_app()` calls `shiny::runApp()`, which starts a server and blocks the R session. The `library(sap)` call does a second job: `shinylive` scans `app.R` for `library()` calls to decide which binaries to bundle. Exporting and previewing take two lines: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} shinylive::export(appdir = "inst/webr", destdir = "_site") httpuv::runStaticServer("_site") ``` ::: Opening `_site/index.html` directly won't work, because `webR` needs its files served over HTTP. ## shinyelectron: the app as a desktop program Some users need the app as a program they install. They might work offline, or their organization might block unknown websites. [Electron](https://www.electronjs.org/) is a framework for desktop programs built with web technologies; an Electron app is just a web browser with a single page. [`shinyelectron`](https://r-pkg.thecoatlessprofessor.com/shinyelectron/) wraps a Shiny app in Electron, so the user never sees a browser or a URL. ### Choosing a runtime strategy The app still needs R, and `shinyelectron` offers five ways to provide it. Each strategy trades installer size against what the user's computer needs: | Strategy | The installer ships | The user needs | |:---|:---|:---| | `shinylive` | Electron and a `webR` bundle | nothing | | `bundled` | Electron and a portable copy of R | nothing | | `auto-download` | Electron and a downloader | internet on first launch | | `system` | Electron only | R installed | | `container` | Electron and a container setup | Docker or Podman | The chapter uses `bundled` for macOS and Windows, which installs `sap` from local source. Portable R only exists for those two platforms, and `bundled` can't cross-build. ### The `electron/` folder The package itself doesn't change. All the desktop code lives in an `electron/` folder: the same launcher `app.R` from the webR chapter, a `_shinyelectron.yml` configuration file, and a `build.R` script. The configuration file holds the setting I found most useful: ```yaml dependencies: r: local_packages: - "../.." ``` `local_packages` installs `sap` from the package root, which is how a `bundled` app gets a package that isn't on CRAN. The CRAN release of `shinyelectron` (0.2.1) doesn't support this field yet, so the chapter installs the development version from GitHub. ### Building the `.dmg` The build script checks the system with `sitrep_shinyelectron()`, validates the app with `app_check()`, and calls `export()`. On an Intel Mac, the result is a `.dmg` of about 256 MB, most of it portable R. Most of the build warnings are harmless. The `NB` notes are worth fixing: `sap` uses the native pipe, so `R CMD build` raised `Depends` to R 4.1.0. :::: {.callout-important collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [Your `.Rprofile` comes along]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} The bundled R reads `~/.Rprofile`. If it calls a package the app doesn't include, the build fails. Wrap those calls in `requireNamespace()`. ::: :::: For Windows, a GitHub Actions matrix runs [`shiny-to-electron`](https://github.com/coatless-actions/shiny-to-electron) on macOS and Windows runners. ### Building the `.deb` The Linux build took the most work. I use Pop!_OS, and `shinyelectron` only builds an `.AppImage` on Linux. `bundled` isn't an option either, because there's no portable R for Linux. The fix combines both chapters. The `shinylive` strategy runs `sap` with `webR` inside the Electron window, which uses the R-universe binary from the webR chapter. `export()` builds the `.AppImage` and leaves an Electron project behind. The build script then edits that project's `package.json` and rebuilds it with `electron-builder`: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 6 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false}}}%% flowchart TD Start(["electron/build.R"]) Export("export() converts the app
to shinylive and builds Electron") AppImage[/".AppImage"/] Project[("electron-app/
Electron project")] Edit("Add the deb target,
homepage, and maintainer") Builder("electron-builder
packages the project") Deb[/".deb"/] Start -->|"i. export"| Export Export --> AppImage Export --> Project Project -->|"ii. edit package.json"| Edit Edit -->|"iii. npx electron-builder"| Builder Builder --> Deb style Start fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style Export fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Edit fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Builder fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 ``` The edit adds three fields, because `electron-builder` refuses to build a `.deb` without a homepage and a maintainer: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} pkg <- jsonlite::read_json(pkg_json) pkg$homepage <- "https://github.com/mjfrigaard/sap" pkg$build$linux$target <- list("AppImage", "deb") pkg$build$linux$maintainer <- "Martin Frigaard " jsonlite::write_json(pkg, pkg_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE) ``` ::: Pop!_OS ships Node.js 18, which is too old. `install_nodejs()` installs a newer version, and `withr::with_path()` puts it ahead of the system version before calling `electron-builder`. After `sudo dpkg -i`, the 183 MB `.deb` adds **Movie Reviews** to the Applications launcher. ## Recap The two chapters take `sap` off the server. `webR` and `shinylive` run it in the browser, with a slower first load and code that every user can see. `shinyelectron` turns it into an installer, with `bundled` R on macOS and Windows and `webR` on Linux. Both start from the same launcher `app.R`, and neither changes the package itself. * [webR chapter](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/webr.html) * [shinyelectron chapter](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/shiny-app-pkgs/shinyelectron.html) * [`sap` repo](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/sap) (branches `22_webr`, `23.1_shinyelectron`, `23.2_shinyelectron-dmg`, and `23.3_shinyelectron-deb`) * [`shinyelectron` docs](https://r-pkg.thecoatlessprofessor.com/shinyelectron/)
